doc.title: Tom Albert and Milton "Mooney" Martin Interview, 1964-12-21

chapter: Trombonists, old string bands and dance steps
title: What the old string-band players did for work, and Tom learning rhythm from a method book
summary: Tom and Russell discuss the day jobs of these musicians and how few bands there were. Tom describes how he learned to divide time with a dollar ABC method book, with Jimmy Palao's help.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Did he have any other job or did he make his living in music? Well, I don't know. I don't know about any job. I know Ford used to play bass. I don't know what he used to do. I think he used to work at the slaughterhouse. Yeah, the slaughterhouse down at the barracks down there. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And so, Mr. Healy did nothing. He played ghetto. Yeah. Buddy Johnson was really a barber then. He had his own barber shop. Yeah. And Joe Big D. You remember Joe Big D? Yeah, I knew Joe Big D. Well, he used to play trombone with us. Key trombone. Yeah, I remember. When I heard him, he played trombone. Well, he had the key trombone. Yeah, he used to play the key trombone with us. We used to go down there together. Well, that old man Joe, he'd be but a hundred and something. He'd be good. Oh, yeah. Yeah, I'm here to see. He was the 30, 50s. Stepfather. Stepfather. Yeah. That's right. But I used to go down to the violins with them fellas all the time. Back to Lake. That's before they had all the bands. They didn't have many bands then. Used to play all around St. Charles Street. I used to play at the school. I used to play all around the school. Me and the bars played when they had the parade. We was playing in the big hall there on St. Charles Street. And they used to give the key. He was an anuset then, you know. And used to come down there and give it to him on the gallery. Well, we used to play that in the day. Yeah. And then we'd play that at night. At night. You see, we'd have a recess after the- The afternoon one. Yeah. We'd come home and then we'd go back that night and play. That's what I said. That's before they had all those bands. They didn't have many bands then. I played all around the- The, what the sick people at the hospital. In the back, all around the hospital. In the back, all around the hospital. Yeah. They'd out and played everywhere they'd be in town. I suppose. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. They'd have a good time, but they didn't have many bands then. Yeah. Yeah. But you also called me the- Paula music. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But everyone, after the Paula music, everybody wanted to play music. Yeah. Yeah. But I learned how to play music. I learned about three months how to divide before I picked up the- Yeah. The violin. The instrument, the carnet, or the violin. The violin. I played violin. Yeah. And I learned then I picked up the violin, but I, I know the division. Mm-hm. And then, you know, I counted with my feet. Yeah. But I learned with my hand though. Yeah. The door rim is- To count it back. Yeah. That's where I, that's the only way I can divide. But this one and two, one and two, uh, look like it's too fast for me. But I did something, got that. Yeah. Yeah. You're counting it forward. Yeah. Yeah. You see, we had a book. Used to be an ABC book. Once it was for that, that sick. We only pay a dollar for it. A method book. A method book. Yeah. Mm-hm. And when you get out of that, probably you know something. Yeah. Yeah. And that's right. That's what I got. Jimmy, he learned me in that book. Yeah. But see, now afterwards, he comes in that one and two, one and two. Well, I never could, uh, divide like that. Mm-hm. But if they say, what is it? That's more fascinating. The, the division's more fascinating.
That was Jimmy Palau, you, you mentioned. Yeah, Jimmy Palau. That helped you with that.
